## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sārambhajātaka* (Ja 88) is a short narrative belonging to the Ekanipāta of the Pali Jātaka collection. The story was delivered by the Buddha while residing at Sāvatthi in connection with the monastic rule against abusive language (*omasavādasikkhāpada*) [Fausböll 1877]. According to the commentary, both the present occasion and the story of the past share the same framework as the preceding *Nandivisālajātaka* (Ja 28) [Fausböll 1877].

The central narrative recounts a past life in which the Bodhisatta was born as a powerful bull named Sārambha [Fausböll 1877]. Out of gratitude to his master, the bull suggests wagering that he can haul one hundred loaded wagons; however, when the master insults and scolds him, the bull refuses to budge, causing the master to lose the bet [Anandajoti 2010]. Only when the master addresses him gently and courteously does the bull exert his strength and successfully win the wager [Anandajoti 2010]. The core moral teaching, preserved in verse, asserts that one should speak only pleasant and harmless words rather than harsh speech (*kalyāṇim eva muñceyya*) [Fausböll 1877; Anandajoti 2010]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the brahmin master as Ānanda, the brahmin's wife as Uppalavaṇṇā, and the ox Sārambha as himself [Fausböll 1877; Paul 1985].
